ex: I can't bear to watch.
차마 못 보겠어.
She couldn't bear to say goodbye.
그녀는 차마 작별 인사를 할 수 없었어.
I can't bear to throw away his letters.
그의 편지를 차마 못 버리겠어.

items.think: When we are "about to" do something, we're **just about to start it, very soon**. "I'm about to leave" means I'm leaving in a minute. "I was just about to call you" means **I was going to do it right then**.
ex: I'm about to leave. Can I call you later?
나 막 나가려던 참이야. 이따 전화해도 돼?
The movie is about to start.
영화 곧 시작해.
I was just about to call you!
막 너한테 전화하려던 참이었어!

items.pic: be forced(힘에 떠밀린 상태) + to(~하는 쪽으로)
items.think: When we "are forced to" do something, we **have no choice but to do it**. Something outside of us is pushing us. People are forced to cancel trips, sell homes, or change plans. It's **not what they wanted**.
ex: We were forced to cancel the trip.
우리는 어쩔 수 없이 여행을 취소해야 했어.
He was forced to sell his house.
그는 집을 팔 수밖에 없었어.
I don't want to be forced to choose.
억지로 선택해야 하는 상황은 싫어.

items.pic: asset(자산, 값진 것) + to(~에게 보탬이 되는)
items.think: When someone is "an asset to" a team or company, they're **very valuable and helpful to it**. An asset is something worth a lot. We often say "**She's a real asset to the team**" to praise someone.
ex: She's a real asset to our team.
그녀는 우리 팀의 진짜 보배야.
Your experience will be an asset to the company.
당신의 경험은 회사에 큰 자산이 될 거예요.
Speaking English is an asset in this job.
이 일에서는 영어 실력이 큰 강점이야.

items.pic: restore(되돌리다) + to(그 지점으로) + former glory(예전의 영광)
items.think: When we "restore something to its former glory," we **bring it back to how amazing it used to be**. People restore old houses, cars, and buildings. Sports teams also try to **return to their former glory**.
ex: They restored the old house to its former glory.
그들은 그 낡은 집을 예전의 멋진 모습으로 복원했어.
The team hopes to return to its former glory.
그 팀은 옛 영광을 되찾길 바라고 있어.
He spent years restoring the car to its former glory.
그는 몇 년에 걸쳐 그 차를 옛 모습 그대로 복원했어.

items.think: When we talk about "the root of" a problem, we mean **its deepest, most basic cause**. Think of a plant's roots under the ground. To fix something, you need to **get to the root of the problem**.
ex: Money is the root of all evil.
돈은 모든 악의 근원이다.
Lack of sleep is the root of the problem.
수면 부족이 문제의 근본 원인이야.
We need to get to the root of this issue.
이 문제의 근본 원인을 파악해야 해.

items.think: When we say "simply put," we're about to **explain something in the easiest way**. It means "to say it simply." People use it after a long explanation to **give the short version**.
ex: Simply put, we're out of money.
간단히 말해서 우리 돈이 없어.
Simply put, the plan didn't work.
쉽게 말하면 그 계획은 실패했어.
Simply put, I love my job.
간단히 말해, 나는 내 일을 사랑해.

items.think: When we say "No wonder," we mean **now I understand why that happened**. It's not surprising anymore. "You worked all night? **No wonder you're tired!**"
ex: No wonder you're tired. You worked all night.
어쩐지 피곤하더라. 밤새 일했잖아.
It's 30 degrees? No wonder I'm sweating.
30도라고? 어쩐지 땀이 나더라.
No wonder she's upset.
그녀가 화난 것도 당연하지.

items.pic: as long as(~만큼 길게 = 그 조건이 이어지는 동안)
items.think: When we say "as long as," we mean **only if this condition is true**. "You can go out as long as you're home by ten" means **you can go, but only with that rule**.
ex: You can go out as long as you're home by 10.
10시까지 들어오기만 하면 나가도 돼.
I don't care what we eat, as long as it's hot.
따뜻하기만 하면 뭘 먹든 상관없어.
As long as we're together, I'm happy.
우리가 함께라면 난 행복해.

items.pic: other than(~ 말고 다른) / apart(떨어져) + from(~에서)
items.think: When we say "other than" or "apart from," we mean **except for that one thing**. "Apart from the rain, the trip was great" means **everything was great except the rain**.
ex: Other than that, everything is fine.
그것 말고는 다 괜찮아.
Apart from the rain, we had a great trip.
비 온 것만 빼면 여행 정말 좋았어.
I don't know anyone here other than you.
여기서 너 말고는 아는 사람이 없어.

items.think: When something is "worth" it, **the result is good enough to justify the cost or effort**. "This movie is worth watching" means you won't regret it. "**It was worth it**" means the hard work paid off.
ex: This movie is worth watching.
이 영화는 볼 만해.
It was hard, but it was worth it.
힘들었지만 그럴 만한 가치가 있었어.
Is it worth the money?
그 돈 낼 만한 가치가 있어?

items.expr: put the cart before the horse
items.pic: put(놓다) + the cart(수레) + before(앞에) + the horse(말)
items.think: When we "put the cart before the horse," we **do things in the wrong order**. A horse should pull the cart, not the other way around. Buying furniture before you have a house is **putting the cart before the horse**.
items.ko: 일의 순서를 거꾸로 하다, 본말이 전도되다
ex: Don't put the cart before the horse. Get the job first.
순서 바꾸지 마. 일자리부터 구해.
Buying furniture before the house is putting the cart before the horse.
집도 없이 가구부터 사는 건 순서가 거꾸로야.
We're putting the cart before the horse with this plan.
이 계획은 앞뒤가 바뀐 것 같아.

items.think: When we "get our mind off" something, we **stop thinking about it for a while**. Usually it's something stressful, like work or a problem. A drink or a movie can **help take your mind off things**.
ex: Let's go grab a drink to get your mind off work.
일 생각 좀 잊게 한잔하러 가자.
You're on vacation! Get your mind off work.
휴가잖아! 일 생각은 좀 잊어.
I watched a movie to get my mind off the exam.
시험 생각 잊으려고 영화를 봤어.

items.think: When we "put something behind us," we **stop thinking about a bad experience and move on**. Picture leaving it behind you as you walk forward. "**Let's put it behind us**" means let's forget it and start fresh.
ex: Let's put it behind us.
그 일은 잊고 넘어가자.
It was a bad year, but I've put it behind me.
힘든 한 해였지만 이제 털어버렸어.
We need to put the argument behind us.
그 말다툼은 이제 잊어야 해.

items.think: When we "take something off someone's shoulders," we **take away some of their stress or responsibility**. Picture lifting a heavy bag off someone's back. It makes them **feel lighter and relieved**.
ex: Let me take some of the responsibility off your shoulders.
책임 좀 내가 덜어 줄게.
Hiring an assistant took a lot off my shoulders.
비서를 뽑았더니 부담이 많이 줄었어.
Finishing the report took a weight off my shoulders.
보고서를 끝내니 어깨가 한결 가벼워졌어.

items.think: When we say "It's no big deal," we mean **it's not important, so don't worry**. People say it when someone apologizes for something small. It **makes the other person feel better**.
ex: Don't worry about it. It's no big deal.
신경 쓰지 마. 별일 아니야.
I'm sorry I'm late. — No big deal.
늦어서 미안해. — 괜찮아.
It's no big deal, but could you close the door?
별건 아닌데, 문 좀 닫아 줄래?

phrasal.title: 🧩 덩어리 표현 (통째로 말하기)
phrasal.core: 문법으로 쪼개지 말고 '말하는 사람의 마음 상태' 하나로 기억하고 입에 붙이기

items.think: When we "are supposed to" do something, it's **expected because of a plan, rule, or promise**. "I'm supposed to meet her at 3" means that's the plan. "You're not supposed to park here" means **it's against the rules**.
ex: I'm supposed to meet her at 3.
나 3시에 그녀를 만나기로 되어 있어.
You're not supposed to park here.
여기 주차하면 안 돼요.
It was supposed to be a surprise!
그거 깜짝 선물이었어야 했는데!

items.think: When we say we "used to" do something, it **was true in the past, but not anymore**. "I used to live in Daegu" means I don't live there now. It **compares the past with the present**.
ex: I used to live in Daegu.
예전에 대구에 살았었어.
I used to smoke, but I quit.
예전엔 담배 피웠는데 끊었어.
There used to be a bakery here.
여기 예전에 빵집이 있었는데.

items.expr: be used to / get used to + -ing
items.pic: be used to(이미 익숙한 상태) / get used to(익숙해지는 중)
items.think: When we "are used to" something, it **feels normal because we've done it a lot**. When we "get used to" something, it's **becoming normal little by little**. "I'm getting used to my new job" means it's getting easier.
ex: I'm used to getting up early.
나는 일찍 일어나는 게 익숙해.
I'm getting used to the new job.
새 일에 점점 익숙해지고 있어.
You'll get used to it.
곧 익숙해질 거야.

items.think: When we "end up" doing something, it's **what finally happened, often not what we planned**. "We ended up taking a taxi" means **that wasn't the original plan**, but that's how it turned out.
ex: I ended up staying home all weekend.
결국 주말 내내 집에 있었어.
We ended up taking a taxi.
결국 택시를 탔어.
He ended up marrying his high school friend.
그는 결국 고등학교 친구와 결혼했어.

items.think: When we say "It turns out," we're **sharing something we discovered later**. It's like turning over a card and seeing the real answer. "**It turns out she's my neighbor**" means I just found that out.
ex: It turns out she's my neighbor.
알고 보니 그녀가 우리 이웃이더라.
It turned out to be a great day.
알고 보니 정말 좋은 하루였어.
It turns out I was wrong.
알고 보니 내가 틀렸더라.

items.pic: can't help(어쩔 수가 없다) + but(~하는 것 말고는)
items.think: When we "can't help but" do something, we **can't stop ourselves from doing it**. It happens naturally, even if we try not to. "I can't help but laugh" means **the laughter just comes out**.
ex: I can't help but laugh at his jokes.
그 사람 농담엔 웃음이 나올 수밖에 없어.
I couldn't help but notice your shoes.
네 신발이 눈에 안 들어올 수가 없었어.
I can't help but worry about her.
그녀가 걱정되는 건 어쩔 수 없어.

items.think: When we say we "might as well" do something, we mean **there's no better option, so let's just do it**. "The bus is late. **We might as well walk**." It's a practical, slightly relaxed choice.
ex: The bus is late. We might as well walk.
버스가 늦네. 그냥 걸어가는 게 낫겠다.
We're here, so we might as well eat.
여기까지 왔으니 먹고 가는 게 낫겠어.
You might as well tell her the truth.
차라리 그녀한테 사실대로 말하는 게 나아.

items.think: When we say "I'd rather," we're **choosing one option over another**. "I'd rather stay home" means **staying home is my preference**. "I'd rather not" is a soft way to say no.
ex: I'd rather stay home tonight.
오늘 밤은 차라리 집에 있을래.
I'd rather walk than take the bus.
버스 타느니 차라리 걸을래.
I'd rather not talk about it.
그 얘기는 안 하고 싶어.

items.think: When we say "I wouldn't mind," we mean **I'd actually like that**. It's a **polite, soft way to say you want something**. "I wouldn't mind a coffee" means I'd happily have one.
ex: I wouldn't mind a cup of coffee.
커피 한잔하면 좋겠는데.
I wouldn't mind living by the sea.
바닷가에 살면 좋겠다.
I wouldn't mind if you joined us.
너도 같이 오면 좋겠어.

items.think: When we're "into" something, we **really like it and enjoy spending time on it**. "I'm into hiking" means it's my hobby. "**I'm not really into horror movies**" is a soft way to say I don't like them.
items.ko: ~에 빠져 있다, ~을 좋아하다 / (not) 별로 안 좋아하다
ex: I'm really into hiking these days.
요즘 등산에 푹 빠져 있어.
I'm not really into horror movies.
공포 영화는 별로 안 좋아해.
What kind of music are you into?
어떤 음악 좋아해?

items.think: When we're "in the middle of" something, we're **busy doing it right now and haven't finished**. "I'm in the middle of something" is a polite way to say **I can't talk right now**.
ex: I'm in the middle of something. Can I call you back?
나 지금 뭐 하는 중이야. 다시 전화해도 돼?
She's in the middle of a meeting.
그녀는 한창 회의 중이야.
We're in the middle of moving.
우리 한창 이사 중이야.

items.think: When we're "sick of" something, we're **tired of it because it's happened too much**. "I'm sick of eating ramen" means **I've had enough**. It's stronger and more emotional than "tired of."
ex: I'm sick of eating ramen every day.
매일 라면 먹는 거 질렸어.
I'm sick of this rain.
이 비 지긋지긋하다.
Aren't you sick of waiting?
기다리는 거 지겹지 않아?

items.pic: be dying(죽을 것 같은) + to(~하고 싶어서)
items.think: When we're "dying to" do something, we **want to do it very, very much**. It's an exaggeration. "I'm dying to see that movie" means **I can't wait to see it**.
ex: I'm dying to see that movie.
그 영화 보고 싶어 죽겠어.
I'm dying to know what happened.
무슨 일이 있었는지 궁금해 죽겠어.
She's dying to meet you.
그녀가 너를 너무 만나고 싶어 해.

items.think: When we say "I can't stand" something, we **really dislike it and can't tolerate it**. "I can't stand the heat" means it bothers me too much. It's **stronger than "I don't like."**
ex: I can't stand the heat.
더위는 정말 못 참겠어.
I can't stand people who lie.
거짓말하는 사람은 질색이야.
I can't stand waiting in line.
줄 서서 기다리는 거 너무 싫어.

items.think: When we say "I take it," we mean **based on what I see, I'm guessing this is true**. It's a way to check your guess. "**I take it you didn't like the food**" means you're reading their reaction.
ex: I take it you didn't like the food.
보아하니 음식이 별로였나 보네.
I take it you two have met before.
두 분 전에 만난 적 있으신가 봐요.
I take it that's a no?
그건 거절이라는 뜻이지?

items.think: When we say "I bet," we mean **I'm pretty sure about this**. It's like you're confident enough to bet money. As a reply, "**I bet!**" means "I can imagine" or "I'm sure that's true."
ex: I bet he's going to be late again.
틀림없이 그 사람 또 늦을 거야.
I bet you're tired after that trip.
그 여행 다녀와서 분명 피곤하겠다.
I was so nervous. — I bet!
나 엄청 긴장했어. — 그랬겠다!

items.think: When we say "I can tell," we mean **I can see it clearly from the signs**. Maybe it's someone's face or voice. "**I can tell you're upset**" means it shows, even if you don't say it.
ex: I can tell you're upset.
너 화난 거 티 나.
I could tell he was lying.
그가 거짓말하는 걸 알 수 있었어.
Can you tell the difference?
차이를 구별할 수 있어?

items.think: When we say "I figured," we mean **I thought about it and guessed this**. "I figured you'd be hungry" means I expected it. "I figured it out" means **I finally solved it**.
ex: I figured you'd be hungry, so I brought food.
너 배고플 것 같아서 음식 가져왔어.
I figured it out!
알아냈어!
I figured as much.
그럴 줄 알았어.

items.think: When we say "I tend to," we mean **I usually do this, it's my habit**. It's not always, but most of the time. "**I tend to forget names**" is a soft way to describe a habit.
ex: I tend to eat too much when I'm stressed.
나는 스트레스 받으면 과식하는 편이야.
I tend to forget names.
나는 이름을 잘 잊어버리는 편이야.
Prices tend to go up in summer.
여름엔 가격이 오르는 경향이 있어.

items.think: When we say "I happen to," we mean **by chance, this is true**. "I happen to know the owner" means it's lucky that I know them. "Do you happen to have a pen?" is a **polite way to ask**.
ex: I happen to know the owner.
내가 마침 사장님을 알아.
Do you happen to have a pen?
혹시 펜 있어?
We happened to be in the same class.
우리는 우연히 같은 반이었어.

items.think: When we say "There's no way," we mean **it's impossible**. "There's no way I can finish today" means it won't happen. "**No way!**" alone can also mean "I can't believe it!"
items.ko: 절대 ~할 리 없다, 말도 안 돼
ex: There's no way I can finish this today.
이걸 오늘 끝낼 방법은 절대 없어.
There's no way he's 50!
그가 쉰 살이라고? 말도 안 돼!
No way! That's amazing.
말도 안 돼! 대박이다.

items.think: When we say "It depends on," we mean **the answer changes based on something else**. "It depends on the weather" means I'll decide later. "**It depends**" alone is a common way to avoid a direct answer.
ex: It depends on the weather.
날씨에 따라 달라.
It depends on how much it costs.
가격이 얼마냐에 달렸어.
Are you coming? — It depends.
올 거야? — 상황 봐서.

items.think: When we say "I owe you," we mean **you helped me, so I need to pay you back someday**. "**I owe you one**" is a friendly thank-you. "How much do I owe you?" is about money.
ex: Thanks for the ride. I owe you one.
태워 줘서 고마워. 신세 졌다.
I owe you an apology.
너한테 사과할 게 있어.
How much do I owe you?
내가 얼마 주면 돼?

items.think: When we're "obsessed with" something, we **can't stop thinking about it**. It can be negative, but in casual talk it often means **we love it a lot**: "I'm obsessed with this song!"
ex: I'm obsessed with this song.
나 이 노래에 완전 꽂혔어.
He's obsessed with his weight.
그는 몸무게에 집착해.
She's obsessed with K-dramas.
그녀는 한국 드라마에 푹 빠져 있어.

items.think: When we ask "What if...?" we're **imagining a possible situation**. It can be a worry: "What if it rains?" Or a suggestion: "What if we stayed home?" It **opens up a new possibility**.
ex: What if it rains tomorrow?
내일 비 오면 어떡해?
What if we just stayed home?
그냥 집에 있으면 어때?
What if I fail the test?
시험에 떨어지면 어쩌지?

items.think: When we ask "How come?" we mean **why?**, but softer and more curious. Native speakers use it a lot. Note: after "How come," we use **normal sentence order**: "How come you didn't call?"
ex: How come you didn't call me?
왜 나한테 전화 안 했어?
How come she's not here?
그녀는 왜 여기 없어?
I'm not going. — How come?
나 안 가. — 왜?

items.think: When we're "all set," we're **completely ready**. Everything is prepared. "I'm all set to go" means I'm ready to leave. Staff also say "**You're all set**" when they've finished helping you.
ex: Are you all set?
준비 다 됐어?
I'm all set to go.
나 갈 준비 다 됐어.
You're all set. Enjoy your stay!
다 처리됐습니다. 즐거운 시간 보내세요!

phrasal.title: ➕ ⬆ UP (추가분)
phrasal.core: 위로 ↑ → ① 집어 올림  ② 드러나 나타남  ③ 끝까지 채움 = 완료·완성  ④ 바짝 다가가 맞섬·따라붙음

items.think: When we "pick something up," we **lift it from a lower place with our hands**. The same picture works for people: you pick someone up when you **give them a ride**. You can also pick up a skill **without really studying**, just by being around it. And when the phone rings, you pick up.
items.ko: 집어 들다 / 데리러 가다 / (기술을) 익히다 / 전화를 받다
ex: Can you pick me up at the station?
역으로 나 데리러 와 줄래?
I picked up some Spanish while traveling.
여행하면서 스페인어를 좀 익혔어.
He didn't pick up when I called.
내가 전화했는데 그가 안 받았어.

items.think: When we "mess up," we **make a mistake and ruin something**. Picture a clean room turned upside down. You can mess up a test, a plan, or even someone's hair. It's a very casual, everyday way to say **"I did it wrong."**
ex: I really messed up the presentation.
발표를 완전히 망쳤어.
Don't mess up my hair!
내 머리 헝클지 마!
Everyone messes up sometimes.
누구나 가끔 실수해.

items.think: When numbers "add up," we **put them together to get a total**. Small things can add up to **something big over time**, like coffee money. When a story "doesn't add up," the pieces **don't fit together**, so it seems false.
ex: Can you add up these numbers?
이 숫자들 좀 합산해 줄래?
Small costs add up quickly.
작은 비용도 금방 쌓여.
His story just doesn't add up.
그의 이야기는 앞뒤가 안 맞아.

items.think: When we "loosen up," we **let go of tension in our body or mind**. Picture a tight knot becoming loose. Friends tell you to loosen up when you're **too serious or nervous**. Athletes also loosen up their muscles before a game.
ex: Loosen up! It's just a party.
긴장 풀어! 그냥 파티잖아.
Let's loosen up before we run.
뛰기 전에 몸 좀 풀자.
He loosened up after a few drinks.
그는 몇 잔 마시고 나서 긴장이 풀렸어.

items.think: When we "brush up on" something, we **practice a skill we used to know but got rusty at**. Picture brushing dust off an old tool so it shines again. People often brush up on a language **before a trip** or on math before an exam.
ex: I need to brush up on my English before the trip.
여행 전에 영어 좀 다시 다듬어야 해.
She's brushing up on her driving skills.
그녀는 운전 실력을 다시 연습하고 있어.
Brush up on the basics first.
기초부터 먼저 복습해.

items.think: When we "take up" a hobby, we **start doing it regularly**. You pick it up and make it part of your life. Things can also take up space or time, which means they **use or fill it**. A big sofa takes up a lot of room.
ex: I took up yoga last year.
작년에 요가를 시작했어.
This sofa takes up too much space.
이 소파는 자리를 너무 많이 차지해.
I don't want to take up your time.
시간 뺏고 싶지 않아요.

items.think: When something "pops up," it **appears suddenly, without warning**. Picture toast jumping out of a toaster. Messages pop up on your screen, problems pop up at work, and new shops **pop up all over town**.
ex: A message popped up on my screen.
화면에 메시지가 떴어.
New cafes keep popping up around here.
이 근처에 새 카페가 계속 생겨.
If any problems pop up, call me.
문제가 생기면 전화해.

items.think: When we "stock up on" something, we **buy a lot of it to use later**. Picture filling the shelves of a store room. People stock up on water before a storm or on snacks before a long weekend. It's about **being ready in advance**.
ex: Let's stock up on water before the storm.
폭풍 오기 전에 물 좀 사 두자.
I stocked up on snacks for the weekend.
주말용 간식을 잔뜩 사 놨어.
People are stocking up on masks.
사람들이 마스크를 비축하고 있어.

items.think: "Make up" is about **putting pieces together into one whole**. You can make up a story, which means you **invent it**. Parts make up a group, so women might make up half a team. And after a fight, two people make up when they **become friends again**.
ex: Stop making up excuses.
핑계 좀 그만 지어내.
Women make up half of our team.
우리 팀의 절반은 여성이야.
They fought, but they made up the next day.
그들은 싸웠지만 다음 날 화해했어.

items.pic: make up(빈 곳을 채워 완성) + for(~에 대한 대가로)
items.think: When we "make up for" something, we **do something good to balance out something bad**. Picture filling a hole so the ground is flat again. You make up for being late by buying lunch, or you **make up for lost time** by working extra hard.
ex: How can I make up for being late?
늦은 거 어떻게 만회하면 될까?
I'm working hard to make up for lost time.
잃어버린 시간을 만회하려고 열심히 하고 있어.
Nothing can make up for that mistake.
그 실수는 무엇으로도 메울 수 없어.

items.pic: make up(깨진 것을 다시 붙여 완성) + with(그 사람과)
items.think: When we "make up with" someone, we **end a fight and become friends again**. The relationship was broken, and now you **put it back together**. Couples and siblings often make up with each other after an argument.
ex: Did you make up with your sister?
언니랑 화해했어?
I want to make up with him before he leaves.
그가 떠나기 전에 화해하고 싶어.
They made up with each other over dinner.
그들은 저녁을 먹으며 서로 화해했어.

items.think: When we "stand up for" someone, we **defend them when others attack**. Picture standing up from your chair to say, "Hey, that's not fair!" You can also stand up for yourself or for **what you believe is right**.
ex: Thanks for standing up for me.
내 편 들어줘서 고마워.
You have to stand up for yourself.
너 자신은 스스로 지켜야 해.
She always stands up for what she believes.
그녀는 늘 자기 신념을 지켜.

items.think: When we "stand up to" someone, we **face a stronger person and refuse to back down**. You stand up tall and look straight at them. People stand up to bullies, bosses, or anyone who **tries to push them around**.
ex: He finally stood up to his boss.
그는 마침내 상사에게 맞섰어.
It takes courage to stand up to bullies.
괴롭히는 애들에게 맞서려면 용기가 필요해.
Stand up to them. Don't let them push you around.
맞서. 그 사람들한테 휘둘리지 마.

items.pic: keep up(뒤처지지 않게 따라붙음) + with(~와 나란히)
items.think: When we "keep up with" something, we **move at the same speed so we don't fall behind**. Picture running next to a fast friend. You can keep up with a person, with your classes, or with **news and trends that change quickly**.
ex: I can't keep up with you. Slow down!
너 못 따라가겠어. 천천히 가!
It's hard to keep up with the news.
뉴스를 다 따라가기 힘들어.
She works hard to keep up with her classmates.
그녀는 반 친구들을 따라가려고 열심히 해.

items.pic: put up(떠받쳐 들고 있음) + with(~을 안고 함께)
items.think: When we "put up with" something, we **accept something annoying without complaining too much**. Picture holding a heavy bag and refusing to drop it. You put up with noisy neighbors or a difficult coworker **because you have no choice**.
ex: I can't put up with this noise anymore.
이 소음 더는 못 참겠어.
How do you put up with him?
그 사람을 어떻게 견뎌?
We had to put up with a long delay.
우리는 긴 지연을 참아야 했어.

items.pic: come up(수면 위로 떠오름) + with(~을 가지고)
items.think: When we "come up with" something, we **think of a new idea, plan, or answer**. Picture an idea rising up from deep in your mind. We use it for creative thinking: you come up with a name, **a solution, or an excuse**.
ex: She came up with a great idea.
그녀가 좋은 아이디어를 냈어.
We need to come up with a plan.
우리는 계획을 세워야 해.
I couldn't come up with an answer.
답이 떠오르지 않았어.

items.think: When we "check up on" someone, we **go and see if they're okay**. Parents check up on kids, and nurses check up on patients. It shows **care, but it can feel like watching** if you do it too often.
ex: I'm just calling to check up on you.
그냥 너 잘 있나 확인하려고 전화했어.
The nurse checks up on him every hour.
간호사가 매시간 그의 상태를 살펴.
Stop checking up on me. I'm fine.
그만 확인해. 나 괜찮아.

phrasal.title: ➕ ⬇ DOWN · ↗ OFF (추가분)
phrasal.core: DOWN = 아래로 가라앉아 자리 잡음·눌림  |  OFF = 붙어 있던 곳에서 떨어져 나감(분리·연기·끝까지 털어 냄)

items.think: When we "settle down," we **become calm and still after a lot of movement**. Picture dust slowly falling to the ground. A noisy class settles down, and so do worries. People also settle down when they **start a stable life**, often with a home and family.
ex: Settle down, everyone. Class is starting.
모두 조용히 해. 수업 시작한다.
They want to settle down and have kids.
그들은 정착해서 아이를 갖고 싶어 해.
Things will settle down soon.
곧 상황이 진정될 거야.

items.pic: come down(아래로 내려와 쓰러짐) + with(~을 안고)
items.think: When we "come down with" an illness, we **start to get sick, usually with something minor**. Picture your energy dropping down as a cold takes over. We often say, "I think I'm **coming down with something**" when we feel the first signs.
ex: I think I'm coming down with a cold.
감기 걸리려나 봐.
Half the office came down with the flu.
사무실 절반이 독감에 걸렸어.
She came down with a fever last night.
그녀는 어젯밤 열이 났어.

items.think: When we "hold off," we **wait before doing something**. Picture holding a door shut so it doesn't open yet. You hold off on a big purchase until prices drop. Rain can also hold off, which means it **doesn't start yet**.
ex: Let's hold off on buying a car.
차 사는 건 좀 미루자.
Can you hold off for a few minutes?
몇 분만 기다려 줄래?
The rain held off until the evening.
비가 저녁까지는 오지 않았어.

items.pic: show(보여 주다) + off(내게서 떨어져 밖으로 확 펼침)
items.think: When we "show off," we **try to make people notice how good, rich, or skilled we are**. Picture someone waving their new watch in everyone's face. It's usually **a little negative**, but you can also proudly show off something nice, like a new baby.
ex: He loves showing off his new car.
그는 새 차 자랑하는 걸 좋아해.
Stop showing off!
그만 잘난 척해!
She showed off her dance moves at the party.
그녀는 파티에서 춤 실력을 뽐냈어.

items.think: When we "pay off" a debt, we **pay all of it until nothing is left**. The loan is finally off your back. Hard work can also pay off, which means it **brings good results in the end**. Your effort was worth it.
ex: I finally paid off my student loan.
드디어 학자금 대출을 다 갚았어.
All your hard work will pay off.
네가 고생한 거 다 보상받을 거야.
The risk paid off.
그 모험은 성공했어.

items.think: When we "top off" a glass or a tank, we **fill it all the way to the top**. We also top off a great day with something special, which means we **finish it in a perfect way**, like dessert at the end of a meal.
ex: Can you top off my coffee?
커피 좀 더 채워 줄래요?
We topped off the night with dessert.
디저트로 그날 밤을 마무리했어.
Let me top off the gas tank.
기름 가득 채울게.

items.think: When we "put something off," we **move it to a later time because we don't want to do it now**. Picture pushing a task far away from today. Something can also put you off, which means it **makes you dislike it**, like a rude waiter.
ex: Stop putting off your homework.
숙제 좀 그만 미뤄.
The meeting was put off until Friday.
회의가 금요일로 연기됐어.
His rude attitude really put me off.
그의 무례한 태도에 정말 정떨어졌어.

items.think: When we "come off as" something, it's **how other people see us, not how we really are**. You might be shy, but you come off as cold. We often use it when we're **worried about giving the wrong impression**.
ex: I don't want to come off as rude.
무례하게 보이고 싶지 않아.
He comes off as shy, but he's really funny.
그는 수줍어 보이지만 사실 정말 웃겨.
Did I come off as angry?
내가 화난 것처럼 보였어?

phrasal.title: ➕ ➡ OUT (추가분)
phrasal.core: 안 → 밖으로 → ① 밖으로 꺼내 드러냄  ② 무리에서 빼냄  ③ 끝까지 다 해서 바닥남·해결

items.think: When we "leave something out," we **don't include it**, either by mistake or on purpose. You can leave out a detail, an ingredient, or a person. If you feel left out, you feel **like everyone forgot about you**.
ex: Don't leave out any details.
세부 사항 하나도 빠뜨리지 마.
I felt left out at the party.
파티에서 소외된 느낌이었어.
You can leave out the sugar.
설탕은 빼도 돼.

items.pic: make(만들어 내다) + out(흐릿한 것에서 밖으로 끄집어냄)
items.think: When we "make something out," we **manage to see, hear, or understand it with difficulty**. Picture squinting at a sign in the fog until the words appear. We usually use it in the negative: "I **can't make out** what he's saying."
ex: I can't make out what he's saying.
그가 뭐라는지 알아들을 수가 없어.
Can you make out that sign?
저 표지판 보여?
I couldn't make out his handwriting.
그의 글씨를 알아볼 수 없었어.

items.think: When we "cross something out," we **draw a line through words to show they're wrong or done**. It's what you do on a to-do list or a test. The words are still there, but they're **officially removed**.
ex: Cross out the wrong answers.
틀린 답은 줄 그어 지워.
I crossed out his name from the list.
명단에서 그의 이름을 지웠어.
She crossed out a word and wrote another.
그녀는 한 단어를 지우고 다른 걸 썼어.

items.think: When we "pick something out," we **choose one thing from a group**. Picture reaching into a box and taking out the best one. You pick out clothes, gifts, or furniture. You can also pick someone out of a crowd when you **recognize them quickly**.
ex: Help me pick out a gift for Mom.
엄마 선물 고르는 것 좀 도와줘.
She picked out a red dress.
그녀는 빨간 드레스를 골랐어.
I could pick you out in any crowd.
어떤 인파 속에서도 널 알아볼 수 있어.

items.pic: figure(계산하다, 그림을 그리다) + out(답을 밖으로 꺼냄)
items.think: When we "figure something out," we **think about it until we understand it or solve it**. Picture working on a puzzle until the answer comes out. It's one of the most common phrases in daily English: "**We'll figure it out**" means don't worry, we'll find a way.
ex: I can't figure out how this works.
이게 어떻게 돌아가는지 모르겠어.
We'll figure it out together.
우리 같이 방법을 찾아보자.
Did you figure out the answer?
답 알아냈어?

items.think: When we "check something out," we **look at it because it's interesting**. "Check this out!" means **look at this!** At a hotel, you check out when you **leave and pay**. At a library, you check out books to borrow them.
ex: Check out this video!
이 영상 좀 봐!
We need to check out by 11.
11시까지 체크아웃해야 해.
I checked out three books from the library.
도서관에서 책 세 권을 빌렸어.

items.think: When we "fill out" a form, we **write information in all the empty spaces**. Picture filling every blank box, from top to bottom. We fill out applications, surveys, and paperwork. In British English, people often say **"fill in"** instead.
ex: Please fill out this form.
이 양식을 작성해 주세요.
I filled out the application online.
온라인으로 지원서를 작성했어.
It took an hour to fill out all the paperwork.
서류를 다 작성하는 데 한 시간 걸렸어.

items.think: When we "point something out," we **make someone notice something they missed**. Picture pointing your finger at it. You can point out a mistake, a fact, or a building. It's a **polite way to show or correct** something.
ex: Thanks for pointing out my mistake.
내 실수 짚어 줘서 고마워.
She pointed out that we were late.
그녀는 우리가 늦었다고 지적했어.
Can you point out where we are on the map?
지도에서 우리가 어디 있는지 짚어 줄래?

items.think: When someone "passes out," they **suddenly lose consciousness and fall**. It can happen from heat, shock, or too much alcohol. We also say it when someone is **so tired they fall asleep instantly**. A teacher can pass out papers, which means **hand them to everyone**.
ex: He passed out from the heat.
그는 더위에 쓰러졌어.
I was so tired I passed out on the sofa.
너무 피곤해서 소파에서 곯아떨어졌어.
The teacher passed out the tests.
선생님이 시험지를 나눠 줬어.

items.pic: work(애써 움직이다) + out(끝까지 → 결과가 밖으로 나옴)
items.think: "Work out" means **putting in effort until you get a result**. When you exercise, you work out. When a problem has an answer, you work it out. And when a situation ends well, we say **it worked out**. "It'll all work out" is a very comforting thing to say.
ex: I work out three times a week.
나는 일주일에 세 번 운동해.
Don't worry. Everything will work out.
걱정 마. 다 잘 풀릴 거야.
We need to work out a solution.
해결책을 찾아내야 해.

items.think: When we "sort something out," we **organize it or fix a problem**. Picture separating a messy pile into neat groups. You sort out your closet, your schedule, or a misunderstanding. It means **making things clear and in order again**.
ex: Let me sort out this mess.
이 난장판 내가 정리할게.
Did you sort out the problem with the bank?
은행 문제는 해결했어?
I need to sort out my closet.
옷장 정리 좀 해야겠어.

items.think: When we "are out of" something, we **have none left**. The box is empty. "We're out of milk" is very common. Stores say items are **out of stock**. A person can also be out of the office, meaning **not there right now**.
ex: We're out of milk.
우유 다 떨어졌어.
Sorry, that item is out of stock.
죄송해요, 그 상품은 품절이에요.
She's out of the office today.
그녀는 오늘 사무실에 없어.

items.think: When we "talk someone out of" something, we **use words to stop them from doing it**. They had a plan, and you pull them out of it with good reasons. It's **the opposite of "talk into"**.
ex: She talked me out of quitting my job.
그녀가 내가 회사 그만두는 걸 말렸어.
Don't try to talk me out of it.
나 말리려고 하지 마.
I talked him out of buying that car.
그가 그 차 사는 걸 내가 말렸어.

phrasal.title: ➕ ⇠ AWAY · ↩ BACK · ↻ AROUND (추가분)
phrasal.core: AWAY = 멀리 떨어뜨림·없앰  |  BACK = 뒤로 물러남·억누름  |  AROUND = 빙 둘러 돌아옴·주변에 머묾

items.think: When we "take something away," we **remove it from a place or a person**. A waiter takes away plates. Something sad can take away your joy. We also talk about what we **take away from an experience**, which is the lesson we keep.
ex: Can you take away these dishes?
이 접시들 좀 치워 줄래요?
Nothing can take away my happiness.
그 무엇도 내 행복을 빼앗을 수 없어.
What did you take away from the class?
그 수업에서 뭘 얻었어?

items.think: When the wind "blows something away," it **carries it far off**. We use the same picture for strong feelings: if a performance blows you away, you are **extremely impressed**. It's like your mind was blown off its feet.
items.ko: 날려 버리다 / 깜짝 놀라게 하다, 감동시키다
ex: The wind blew away my hat.
바람에 모자가 날아갔어.
Her voice blew me away.
그녀의 목소리에 완전 반했어.
I was blown away by the view.
경치를 보고 넋이 나갔어.

items.think: When we "put something away," we **return it to its proper place so it's out of sight**. You put away dishes, clothes, or your phone. You can also put away money, which means **saving it for later**.
ex: Put away your toys.
장난감 치워.
Please put your phones away during class.
수업 중에는 휴대폰을 넣어 주세요.
I put away some money every month.
매달 돈을 조금씩 모아 둬.

items.think: When we "walk away," we **leave a person or situation instead of staying**. Picture turning around and walking off. Sometimes it's rude, but sometimes it's smart: you can **walk away from a bad deal** or an argument.
ex: Don't just walk away from me!
그냥 가 버리지 마!
Sometimes it's better to walk away.
가끔은 그냥 떠나는 게 나아.
He walked away from a great job.
그는 좋은 직장을 박차고 나왔어.

items.think: When we "give something away," we **give it for free**. Stores give away samples. But you can also give away **a secret or the ending of a movie**, by accident. Your face can give away your feelings, too.
ex: They're giving away free samples.
무료 샘플을 나눠 주고 있어.
Don't give away the ending!
결말 말하지 마!
His face gave away his feelings.
얼굴에 감정이 다 드러났어.

items.pic: get away(빠져나가 멀리 도망침) + with(~을 가진 채)
items.think: When we "get away with" something, we **do something wrong and don't get punished**. Picture a thief running away with the money. Parents say, "**You won't get away with this!**" when they're angry.
ex: You won't get away with this!
이러고도 무사할 줄 알아?
He always gets away with being late.
그는 늘 지각해도 그냥 넘어가.
She cheated and got away with it.
그녀는 부정행위를 하고도 안 걸렸어.

items.think: When we "stay away from" something, we **keep a safe distance from it**. You stay away from danger, bad food, or people who hurt you. It's a strong way to say **avoid it completely**.
ex: Stay away from my sister!
내 여동생한테 가까이 오지 마!
I try to stay away from junk food.
정크 푸드는 멀리하려고 해.
Stay away from the edge.
가장자리에서 떨어져.

items.think: When we "cut back on" something, we **use or do less of it**. Picture trimming a plant so it's smaller. People cut back on sugar, spending, or screen time when they want to **be healthier or save money**.
ex: I'm trying to cut back on coffee.
커피를 줄이려고 하고 있어.
We need to cut back on spending.
지출을 줄여야 해.
The doctor told him to cut back on salt.
의사가 그에게 소금을 줄이라고 했어.

items.think: When we "hold back," we **stop ourselves from showing or doing something**. You hold back tears, laughter, or the truth. Fear can also hold you back, which means it **stops you from moving forward** in life.
ex: She couldn't hold back her tears.
그녀는 눈물을 참을 수 없었어.
Don't hold back. Tell me everything.
숨기지 말고 다 말해 줘.
Fear is holding you back.
두려움이 너를 붙잡고 있어.

items.think: When someone "comes around," they **finally change their mind and agree**. Picture someone walking a long way around before arriving at your side. It also means to **visit someone's home**, as in "Come around for dinner."
ex: Don't worry. He'll come around.
걱정 마. 그도 결국 마음을 바꿀 거야.
She finally came around to my idea.
그녀가 마침내 내 생각에 동의했어.
Come around for dinner sometime.
언제 저녁 먹으러 들러.

items.think: When we "stick around," we **stay in a place a little longer instead of leaving**. It's casual and friendly. "Stick around!" means **don't go yet**. You can also wonder if a new trend will stick around.
ex: Stick around. The fun is just starting.
좀 더 있어. 이제 막 재밌어지려고 해.
I can't stick around. I have to go.
오래 못 있어. 가야 해.
Will you stick around after the show?
공연 끝나고도 남아 있을 거야?

items.think: When we "pass something around," we **hand it from person to person in a group**. Picture a plate of cookies going around a table. Information can be passed around too, like **a rumor spreading through an office**.
ex: Please pass around these handouts.
이 유인물 좀 돌려 주세요.
We passed around the photos.
우리는 사진을 돌려 봤어.
The rumor was passed around the office.
그 소문이 사무실에 쫙 돌았어.

phrasal.title: ➕ ↘ IN · ● ON · ⌒ OVER · ⟶ THROUGH (추가분)
phrasal.core: IN/INTO = 안으로 쏙 들어감  |  ON = 붙어서 기댐  |  OVER = 위로 훑거나 넘어감  |  THROUGH = 처음부터 끝까지 통과

items.think: When we "fit in," we **feel comfortable and accepted in a group**. Picture a puzzle piece sliding into the right spot. New students often worry about fitting in. You can also fit someone in, which means **find time for them in a busy schedule**.
ex: I didn't fit in at my old school.
예전 학교에선 잘 어울리지 못했어.
She fits in well with the team.
그녀는 팀에 잘 녹아들어.
Can you fit me in this afternoon?
오늘 오후에 저 좀 끼워 주실 수 있어요?

items.think: When we "blend in," we **look similar to the things around us so we don't stand out**. Picture paint mixing until you can't see where one color ends. Tourists try to blend in with locals. It's **the opposite of "stand out."**
items.ko: (주변에) 섞여 들다, 눈에 안 띄게 녹아들다
ex: I wore black to blend in.
눈에 안 띄려고 검은 옷을 입었어.
The new building blends in with the old town.
새 건물이 구시가지와 잘 어우러져.
Chameleons blend in with their surroundings.
카멜레온은 주변과 섞여 들어.

items.think: When we "tap into" something, we **start using a resource that was already there**. Picture putting a tap into a barrel to let water flow. Businesses tap into new markets, and people **tap into their creativity** or hidden talent.
ex: We need to tap into new markets.
새로운 시장을 개척해야 해.
Music helps me tap into my emotions.
음악은 내 감정을 끌어내 줘.
Tap into your creativity.
네 창의력을 끌어내 봐.

items.think: When we "talk someone into" something, we **persuade them to do it**, often when they didn't want to at first. You pull them into the plan with your words. "**She talked me into it**" means it wasn't really my idea.
ex: She talked me into going to the party.
그녀가 날 설득해서 파티에 가게 했어.
Don't let him talk you into it.
그가 그걸 하라고 설득해도 넘어가지 마.
I got talked into buying a new phone.
설득당해서 새 폰을 샀어.

items.think: "Get into" means **entering a place or a situation**. You get into a car or a good school. You can get into a hobby when you **start to really enjoy it**. And you can get into trouble, which means **a bad situation starts**.
ex: Get into the car!
차에 타!
I got into yoga last year.
작년에 요가에 빠졌어.
You'll get into trouble.
너 혼날 거야.

items.think: When we "run into" someone, we **meet them by chance**. Picture turning a corner and almost bumping into them. We also run into problems, which means we **suddenly face difficulties** we didn't expect.
ex: I ran into my ex at the mall.
쇼핑몰에서 전 애인을 우연히 마주쳤어.
We ran into some problems.
우리는 몇 가지 문제에 부딪혔어.
Guess who I ran into today!
오늘 누구 만났는지 맞혀 봐!

items.think: When we "count on" someone, we **trust that they will help us or do what they promised**. "You can count on me" is a strong promise. It means **I won't let you down**.
ex: You can count on me.
나만 믿어.
I'm counting on you to finish this.
이거 끝내는 거 너만 믿을게.
Don't count on the weather.
날씨는 믿지 마.

items.pic: rely(믿고 맡기다) + on(~ 위에 몸을 얹음)
items.think: When we "rely on" something, we **depend on it because we need it**. Picture leaning your full weight on a strong wall. People rely on friends, phones, or buses. It's a little **more formal than "count on"**.
ex: I rely on my phone too much.
나는 휴대폰에 너무 의존해.
You can always rely on her.
그녀는 언제나 믿어도 돼.
Many people rely on public transport.
많은 사람이 대중교통에 의지해.

items.think: When we "look something over," we **check it quickly from top to bottom**. Picture your eyes moving over a page. You ask someone to look over your essay before you submit it. It's **faster and lighter than a full review**.
ex: Could you look over my essay?
내 에세이 좀 봐 줄래?
I looked over the contract last night.
어젯밤에 계약서를 훑어봤어.
Let me look it over first.
먼저 한번 훑어볼게.

items.think: When we "think something over," we **take time to consider it carefully before deciding**. Picture turning an idea around in your hands. "**Let me think it over**" is a polite way to say you're not ready to answer yet.
ex: Let me think it over.
생각 좀 해 볼게.
Take some time to think over the offer.
그 제안 시간 갖고 생각해 봐.
I thought it over and said yes.
곰곰이 생각해 보고 승낙했어.

items.think: When we "get over" something, we **recover from it and move on**. Picture climbing over a wall that was blocking you. People get over a cold, a breakup, or a bad day. "**Get over it**" is a blunt way to say stop being upset.
ex: It took me months to get over him.
그를 잊는 데 몇 달이 걸렸어.
I just got over a cold.
감기가 막 나았어.
Get over it. It's not a big deal.
그만 잊어. 별일 아니야.

items.think: When we "look through" things, we **go through them one by one to find something or get an idea**. You look through photos, files, or a bag. It's a bit **more searching than "look over"**.
ex: I looked through my old photos.
옛날 사진들을 쭉 훑어봤어.
She looked through her bag for her keys.
그녀는 열쇠를 찾으려고 가방을 뒤졌어.
Can you look through these files?
이 파일들 좀 살펴봐 줄래?

items.think: When we "go through" something, we **move through it from beginning to end**. Picture walking through a dark tunnel. You can go through a hard time, which means **experience it**. You can also go through a list to **check every item**.
items.ko: (힘든 일을) 겪다 / 꼼꼼히 살펴보다 / 다 써 버리다
ex: She's going through a hard time.
그녀는 힘든 시간을 보내고 있어.
Let's go through the plan again.
계획을 다시 한번 살펴보자.
We went through two bottles of water.
우리 물 두 병을 다 마셨어.

items.pic: be through(끝까지 통과해 나옴) + with(~와의 일)
items.think: When we "are through with" something, we **have finished with it completely**. You can be through with a book or a task. When people say "**I'm through with him**," it means the relationship is over.
ex: Are you through with the newspaper?
신문 다 봤어?
I'm through with him.
그 사람이랑은 끝이야.
Call me when you're through with work.
일 끝나면 전화해.

phrasal.title: ➕ ⇢ ASIDE · BEHIND · AHEAD · ACROSS · BY · 전치사 결합 (추가분)
phrasal.core: ASIDE/APART = 옆으로 따로 떼어 둠 | BEHIND/AHEAD = 뒤처짐/앞서감 | ACROSS = 건너편까지 가로질러 닿음 | BY = 곁을 스쳐 지나감 | WITH = 함께 | FOR = 그쪽을 향함 | TO = 그 지점에 닿음

items.think: When we "set something aside," we **put it to one side to save it for later**. People set aside money or time for something important. You can also set aside a feeling or problem, which means **ignore it for now** so you can move on.
items.ko: 따로 떼어 두다, 확보하다 / 제쳐 두다
ex: I set aside some money for the trip.
여행 갈 돈을 따로 떼어 놨어.
Let's set aside our differences.
우리 차이는 잠시 제쳐 두자.
Set aside an hour a day for reading.
하루 한 시간은 독서 시간으로 빼 둬.

items.think: When something "sets you apart," it **makes you different from others in a good way**. Picture one person standing a little apart from the crowd. Interviewers often ask, "**What sets you apart?**"
ex: What sets you apart from other candidates?
다른 지원자와 당신을 구별 짓는 점은 뭔가요?
Her voice sets her apart.
그녀는 목소리 때문에 돋보여.
Good service sets this hotel apart.
좋은 서비스가 이 호텔을 특별하게 만들어.

items.think: When we "fall behind," we **can't keep up and end up behind others**. Picture a runner slowly dropping to the back of the group. Students fall behind in class, and people fall behind **on payments or schedules**.
ex: I fell behind in math class.
수학 수업에서 뒤처졌어.
Don't fall behind on your payments.
납부가 밀리지 않게 해.
We're falling behind schedule.
우리 일정이 밀리고 있어.

items.think: When we "get ahead," we **become more successful than others or than before**. Picture moving to the front of a race. People work hard to get ahead **in their careers**. You can also get ahead on work by doing it early.
ex: He works hard to get ahead.
그는 성공하려고 열심히 일해.
You need good skills to get ahead in this job.
이 일에서 앞서가려면 실력이 좋아야 해.
I want to get ahead on my homework.
숙제를 미리 해 두고 싶어.

items.think: "Go ahead" means **you have permission, so start**. Picture someone stepping aside and waving you forward. It's a friendly answer to "Can I...?" Plans can also go ahead, which means they **happen as planned**.
ex: Can I sit here? — Sure, go ahead.
여기 앉아도 돼요? — 그럼요, 앉으세요.
Go ahead and start without me.
나 없이 먼저 시작해.
The concert will go ahead despite the rain.
콘서트는 비가 와도 진행돼.

items.think: When we "get an idea across," we **make another person understand it**. Picture sending your idea across a river to someone on the other side. Good teachers know how to **get their message across clearly**.
ex: I couldn't get my point across.
내 요점을 전달하지 못했어.
Pictures help get the message across.
그림은 메시지를 전달하는 데 도움이 돼.
How can I get this across to him?
이걸 그에게 어떻게 이해시키지?

items.think: When we "come across" something, we **find it by chance**. It crosses your path while you're doing something else. People can also come across as kind or rude, which is **the impression they give to others**.
ex: I came across an old letter.
오래된 편지를 우연히 발견했어.
She comes across as very confident.
그녀는 매우 자신감 있어 보여.
Have you ever come across this word?
이 단어 본 적 있어?

items.think: When we "get by," we **manage to live or survive with just enough**. Picture squeezing past something in a narrow hallway. It's not comfortable, but **you make it work**. You can get by on a small salary or with basic English.
ex: I can get by on a small salary.
적은 월급으로도 그럭저럭 살 수 있어.
My Spanish is enough to get by.
내 스페인어는 그럭저럭 지낼 정도는 돼.
How do you get by without a car?
차 없이 어떻게 지내?

items.think: When we "do without" something, we **manage even though we don't have it**. "I can't do without coffee" means **I really need it**. Sarcastically, "I could do without that" means **I don't want it at all**.
ex: I can't do without coffee in the morning.
아침엔 커피 없이는 못 살아.
We'll have to do without a car.
우리 차 없이 지내야 할 거야.
I could do without his comments.
그의 참견은 없어도 돼(안 했으면 좋겠어).

items.think: When we "mingle with" people, we **move around and talk to many people at an event**. Picture yourself mixing into the crowd at a party. Hosts often say, "**Go mingle!**" to encourage guests to meet each other.
ex: Go mingle with the other guests.
다른 손님들이랑 좀 어울려 봐.
I'm not good at mingling with strangers.
나는 낯선 사람들과 잘 못 어울려.
The singer mingled with fans after the show.
가수가 공연 후 팬들과 어울렸어.

items.think: When we "get along with" someone, we **have a friendly, easy relationship with them**. Picture two people walking along the same path together. It's how we talk about coworkers, roommates, or family: **"We get along great."**
ex: Do you get along with your coworkers?
동료들이랑 잘 지내?
My cat doesn't get along with dogs.
우리 고양이는 개랑 사이가 안 좋아.
We get along really well.
우리 정말 잘 지내.

items.think: "Go with" means **two things belong together** or **you choose one option**. Shoes can go with a dress, and wine goes with food. At a restaurant, "**I'll go with the pasta**" means I choose the pasta.
ex: Does this tie go with my shirt?
이 넥타이 내 셔츠랑 어울려?
I'll go with the chicken.
저는 치킨으로 할게요.
Red wine goes well with steak.
레드 와인은 스테이크랑 잘 어울려.

items.think: When we "go for" something, we **choose it or try hard to get it**. Picture running toward a goal. "I'll go for the salad" is a choice. "**Go for it!**" means try it, don't be afraid. It can also describe **the type of person you like**.
ex: I'll go for the blue one.
파란 걸로 할게.
If you want the job, go for it.
그 일 원하면 도전해 봐.
She usually goes for tall guys.
그녀는 보통 키 큰 남자를 좋아해.

items.think: When we "fall for" someone, we **suddenly fall in love with them**. Picture tripping and falling right into their arms. You can also fall for a trick or a lie, which means you **believe it and get fooled**.
ex: I fell for her the moment I saw her.
그녀를 보자마자 반했어.
Don't fall for that trick.
그 수법에 속지 마.
I can't believe I fell for it.
내가 거기에 속다니 믿을 수가 없어.

items.think: When we "take after" a parent, we **look or act like them**. You got their traits as they were passed down to you. "**She takes after her dad**" might mean she has his eyes or his sense of humor.
ex: You really take after your father.
너 정말 아빠 닮았다.
She takes after her mom in looks.
그녀는 외모가 엄마를 닮았어.
Who do you take after more?
넌 누구를 더 닮았어?

items.think: When we "care about" something, we **think it's important and want it to be okay**. You care about people you love and causes you believe in. "**I don't care about that**" means it doesn't matter to me.
ex: I really care about you.
난 정말 네가 소중해.
I don't care about money.
돈엔 관심 없어.
She cares about the environment.
그녀는 환경 문제에 관심이 많아.

items.think: When one thing "comes before" another, it **is earlier in order or more important**. Picture a line where one person stands in front. "**Family comes before work**" is a common way to talk about priorities.
ex: Family comes before work.
가족이 일보다 먼저야.
Safety comes before speed.
속도보다 안전이 우선이야.
Which letter comes before K?
K 앞에 오는 글자는 뭐야?

items.think: "Come to" means **arriving at a point**. A bill comes to a total amount. A person who fainted **comes to** when they wake up. And a situation can come to something bad: "**I never thought it would come to this.**"
ex: The bill comes to $50.
계산서가 50달러 나왔어.
When he came to, he was in the hospital.
그가 정신을 차렸을 때는 병원이었어.
I never thought it would come to this.
일이 이렇게까지 될 줄 몰랐어.

items.think: "Get to" means **reaching a place or a point**. You get to work at nine. It also means **you have the chance to do something nice**: "I got to meet the singer!" And if something gets to you, it **really bothers you**.
ex: How do I get to the station?
역에 어떻게 가요?
I got to meet my favorite singer!
제일 좋아하는 가수를 만나게 됐어!
Don't let him get to you.
그 사람 때문에 신경 쓰지 마.

pattern.title: 🌡 확신의 온도계 (생각·추측)
pattern.core: 영어는 '내가 얼마나 확신하는지'를 문장 맨 앞에 먼저 깔고 내용을 붙인다. 100% I'm sure → 80% I think → 50% I guess·It seems → 20% I doubt → 0% I have no idea

items.expr: I'm sure / I'm certain (that) + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "I'm sure" or "I'm certain," we **show we're 100% confident** before we even give the information. Native speakers put the confidence first, then the fact. "I'm certain" sounds **a little stronger and more formal**.
ex: I'm sure you'll do great.
넌 분명 잘할 거야.
I'm certain that I locked the door.
문 잠근 거 확실해.
Are you sure? — Yes, I'm sure.
확실해? — 응, 확실해.

items.expr: I have no doubt (that) + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "I have no doubt," we mean **there's zero question in my mind**. It's even stronger than "I'm sure." We often use it to **show strong belief in someone**: "I have no doubt you'll do great."
ex: I have no doubt that she'll win.
그녀가 이길 거라는 데 의심의 여지가 없어.
I have no doubt you can do it.
넌 할 수 있다고 굳게 믿어.
He has no doubt about his decision.
그는 자기 결정에 전혀 의심이 없어.

items.think: When we say "I believe," we're sharing **something we think is true, with good reason**. It sounds more serious than "I think." We also use it to **politely state a fact we're fairly sure about**: "I believe the meeting is at 3."
ex: I believe we can solve this.
우리가 이걸 해결할 수 있다고 믿어.
I believe the meeting is at 3.
회의는 3시인 걸로 알고 있어.
I don't believe that's true.
그게 사실이라고 생각하지 않아.

items.expr: I think + 주어 + 동사 / I don't think + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "I think," we **share our opinion without sounding too strong**. Here's the native trick: to be negative, we say "**I don't think** it's a good idea," not "I think it's not a good idea." We **put the 'not' up front**.
ex: I think it's going to rain.
비 올 것 같아.
I don't think he's coming.
그 사람 안 올 것 같아.
I don't think that's a good idea.
그건 좋은 생각 같지 않아.

items.think: When we say "I guess," we're **making a guess without much proof**. It's around 50% sure. We also say "I guess so" when we **agree a little reluctantly**. It sounds relaxed and casual.
items.ko: ~인가 봐, ~인 것 같아(짐작) / 뭐 그런가 보지
ex: I guess you're right.
네 말이 맞는 것 같네.
I guess she's not home.
그녀가 집에 없나 봐.
Are you okay? — I guess so.
괜찮아? — 뭐, 그런 것 같아.

items.expr: It seems + 형용사 / It seems that + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "It seems," we're **describing how something appears to us**. We don't say "I" directly, so it sounds **softer and more objective**. "It seems like everyone's busy" is gentle, not judgmental.
ex: It seems strange.
좀 이상한 것 같아.
It seems that we're lost.
우리 길 잃은 것 같아.
It seems like everyone is busy today.
오늘 다들 바쁜 것 같네.

items.expr: It looks like + 명사 / 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "It looks like," we're **making a guess based on what we can see**. Dark clouds? "It looks like rain." Use it when there's **visual evidence** in front of you.
ex: It looks like it's going to rain.
비가 올 것 같아.
It looks like nobody's here.
여기 아무도 없는 것 같아.
It looks like you've lost weight.
너 살 빠진 것 같아.

items.expr: It sounds like + 명사 / 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "It sounds like," we're **reacting to what someone just told us**. It's based on what we hear. "**That sounds like fun!**" or "It sounds like you had a rough day" shows you're really listening.
ex: It sounds like you had a rough day.
힘든 하루였나 보네.
That sounds like a great plan.
좋은 계획 같아.
It sounds like someone's at the door.
누가 문 앞에 온 것 같아.

items.think: When we say "As far as I know," we mean **this is true based on my knowledge, but I might be wrong**. It's a polite safety net. It lets you **share information without promising it's 100% correct**.
ex: As far as I know, the store is open until 9.
내가 알기로는 그 가게 9시까지 열어.
As far as I know, he's still single.
내가 알기론 그 사람 아직 싱글이야.
Nobody told me, as far as I know.
내가 아는 한 아무도 나한테 말 안 했어.

items.expr: I have a feeling (that) + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "I have a feeling," we're **sharing a guess based on our gut, not facts**. You can't explain why, you just feel it. "**I have a bad feeling about this**" is a classic line.
ex: I have a feeling we'll meet again.
왠지 우리 또 만날 것 같아.
I have a bad feeling about this.
이거 왠지 느낌이 안 좋아.
I had a feeling you'd say that.
네가 그렇게 말할 줄 알았어.

items.think: When we say "I doubt," we mean **I don't think this will happen**. It's about 20% sure. "I doubt he'll come" means **he probably won't come**. "I doubt it" alone is a common short answer.
ex: I doubt he'll come.
그 사람 안 올 것 같아.
I doubt it.
글쎄, 아닐걸.
I doubt that we can finish today.
오늘 끝낼 수 있을지 의문이야.

items.think: When we say "I wonder if," we're **thinking out loud about something we're curious about**. It's softer than a direct question. It also works as **a gentle way to ask** without pressuring someone.
ex: I wonder if she got my message.
그녀가 내 메시지 받았을까?
I wonder if it'll snow tomorrow.
내일 눈이 올까?
I wonder why he left early.
그 사람 왜 일찍 갔는지 궁금하네.

items.think: When we say "I'm not sure," we **admit we don't have a clear answer**. Then we add what we're unsure about: what, if, or how. "**I'm not sure if I should go**" shows you're still deciding.
ex: I'm not sure what to say.
뭐라고 말해야 할지 모르겠어.
I'm not sure if I should go.
가야 할지 말아야 할지 모르겠어.
I'm not sure how it works.
그게 어떻게 작동하는지 잘 모르겠어.

items.think: When we say "I have no idea," we mean **I don't know at all**. It's stronger than "I don't know." There's **not even a small clue** in my head. Very common in everyday conversation.
ex: I have no idea what you're talking about.
네가 무슨 말 하는지 전혀 모르겠어.
I have no idea where my keys are.
열쇠가 어디 있는지 전혀 모르겠어.
Who broke it? — I have no idea.
누가 깼어? — 전혀 몰라.

items.think: When we say "I might," we mean **maybe, it's possible but not decided**. It's around 30–50% likely. "I might be late" warns someone gently. "**You might want to** bring an umbrella" is a soft suggestion.
ex: I might be late tonight.
오늘 밤 좀 늦을지도 몰라.
I might go to the party.
파티에 갈 수도 있어.
You might want to bring an umbrella.
우산 챙기는 게 좋을 수도 있어.

pattern.title: 🎯 마음의 방향 (원함·계획)
pattern.core: 영어는 '원한다/할 거다'를 먼저 말하고 to(→ 화살표) 뒤에 행동을 붙인다. 세기: I'm dying to > I can't wait to > I'd love to > I want to > I'd like to(공손) > I hope to

items.expr: I'd like to + 동사 (= I want to)
items.think: When we say "I'd like to," we're **saying what we want in a polite way**. "I want to" is direct; "I'd like to" is **softer and more professional**. Use it at restaurants, hotels, and work.
ex: I'd like to order now.
지금 주문할게요.
I'd like to make a reservation.
예약하고 싶어요.
I want to go home.
집에 가고 싶어.

items.think: When we say "I wish to," we're **stating what we want very formally**. You'll see it in letters or official situations. In daily talk, it sounds stiff. Don't confuse it with "**I wish I could**," which is about something **not possible**.
ex: I wish to speak to the manager.
매니저님과 이야기하고자 합니다.
We wish to thank everyone for coming.
와 주신 모든 분께 감사드리고자 합니다.
I wish I could stay longer.
더 오래 있을 수 있으면 좋을 텐데.

items.think: When we say "I hope to," we're **talking about something we want to do in the future**. It's possible, but not certain. "I hope to see you again" is **warm and polite**.
ex: I hope to see you again.
또 뵙길 바라요.
She hopes to study abroad next year.
그녀는 내년에 유학 가길 바라.
I hope you feel better soon.
얼른 낫길 바라.

items.think: When we say "I just want to," we mean **this one simple thing is all I want**. "Just" makes it small and honest. It's also used to **clear up a misunderstanding**: "I just wanted to help."
ex: I just want to sleep.
그냥 자고 싶어.
I just want to say thank you.
그냥 고맙다고 말하고 싶었어.
I just wanted to help.
난 그냥 도와주고 싶었을 뿐이야.

items.think: When we say "I'm going to," we're **talking about a plan we've already decided**. We're already on the way toward it. In casual speech, it often sounds like "**I'm gonna**."
ex: I'm going to visit my parents this weekend.
이번 주말에 부모님 댁에 갈 거야.
It's going to rain.
비 올 거야.
I'm gonna grab some coffee.
커피 좀 사 올게.

items.think: When we say "I'm thinking about," we mean **I'm considering it, but I haven't decided yet**. The idea is still in my head. "I'm thinking about changing jobs" means **it's a possibility**.
ex: I'm thinking about changing jobs.
이직할까 생각 중이야.
We're thinking about getting a dog.
우리 강아지 키울까 생각 중이야.
I'm thinking about what to cook.
뭘 요리할지 생각 중이야.

items.think: When we say "I was planning to," we mean **this was my plan before, but something changed** or I'm about to do it. "I was planning to call you" can also mean **I was just about to**.
ex: I was planning to call you tonight.
오늘 밤에 너한테 전화하려고 했었어.
I was planning to stay home, but my friend called.
집에 있으려 했는데 친구가 전화했어.
We were planning to leave early.
우리 일찍 나갈 계획이었어.

items.think: When we say "I'm considering," we're **seriously thinking about the pros and cons**. It's more serious than "thinking about." Remember: after "considering," we use **-ing**, not "to."
ex: I'm considering moving to Busan.
부산으로 이사하는 걸 고려 중이야.
She's considering going back to school.
그녀는 다시 학교에 다니는 걸 고민 중이야.
We're considering all options.
우리는 모든 선택지를 검토 중이에요.

items.think: When we say "I can't wait to," we mean **I'm super excited about something coming up**. Waiting feels too hard. "**I can't wait to see you!**" is full of excitement.
ex: I can't wait to see you!
빨리 보고 싶어!
I can't wait to try that restaurant.
그 식당 빨리 가 보고 싶어.
I can't wait for the weekend.
주말이 너무 기다려져.

items.think: When we say "I'd love to," we're **saying we really want to do something**. It's the best way to **happily accept an invitation**: "Want to come? — I'd love to!" "I'd love to, but..." is a soft no.
ex: Want to join us? — I'd love to!
같이 갈래? — 좋지!
I'd love to visit Japan someday.
언젠가 일본에 꼭 가 보고 싶어.
I'd love to, but I'm busy.
정말 그러고 싶은데 바빠.

items.expr: I feel like + -ing / I feel like + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "I feel like + -ing," we mean **I want to do this right now**: "I feel like eating pizza." When we say "I feel like + sentence," we're **sharing an opinion or feeling**: "I feel like I forgot something."
ex: I feel like eating pizza tonight.
오늘 밤 피자 먹고 싶다.
I don't feel like going out.
나가고 싶지 않아.
I feel like I forgot something.
뭔가 잊어버린 것 같은 느낌이야.

items.think: When we ask "Do you want to...?" we're usually **inviting someone casually**, not just asking about their wants. "Do you want to grab lunch?" means **let's eat together**. Often it sounds like "Wanna...?"
ex: Do you want to grab lunch?
점심 먹으러 갈래?
Do you want to come with me?
나랑 같이 갈래?
Wanna watch a movie?
영화 볼래?

items.think: When we say "I'm trying to," we mean **I'm making an effort, but it's not done yet**. "I'm trying to lose weight" shows you're working on it. "I'm trying to find the station" means **I'm looking for it now**.
ex: I'm trying to lose weight.
살 빼려고 노력 중이야.
I'm trying to find the subway station.
지하철역을 찾는 중이에요.
I'm trying to concentrate.
집중하려는 중이야.

items.think: When we say "I'm trying to avoid," we mean **I'm working hard not to do something**. People avoid sugar, late-night snacks, or traffic. After "avoid," we always use **-ing**.
ex: I'm trying to avoid sugar.
설탕을 피하려고 노력 중이야.
I'm trying to avoid eating late at night.
밤늦게 먹는 걸 피하려고 해.
She's trying to avoid him.
그녀는 그를 피하려고 해.

pattern.title: 🙏 공손의 거리 (부탁·허락)
pattern.core: 영어의 공손함 = '거리 두기'. 현재(can/will) → 과거(could/would)로 한 발 물러설수록, 문장이 길어질수록 더 공손해진다. Can you < Could you < Would you mind < I was just wondering if

items.think: When we ask "Can you...?" we're **asking someone for help in a simple, casual way**. It's perfect for friends and family. It's **friendly but direct**.
ex: Can you help me with this?
이것 좀 도와줄래?
Can you pass me the salt?
소금 좀 건네줄래?
Can you call me back later?
나중에 다시 전화해 줄래?

items.pic: [혹시 ~해 줄 수 있을까요?] (can의 한 발 물러선 형태)
items.think: When we ask "Could you...?" we're **asking for help more politely than "Can you."** "Could" puts a little distance between us, which **makes it softer**. Great for strangers and coworkers.
ex: Could you open the window?
창문 좀 열어 주시겠어요?
Could you say that again?
다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Could you send me the file?
파일 좀 보내 주실 수 있을까요?

items.think: When we ask "Will you...?" we're **asking if someone is willing to do something**. It can sound **a bit direct**, so tone matters. It's also used for big questions, like "**Will you marry me?**"
ex: Will you be home tonight?
오늘 밤 집에 있을 거야?
Will you marry me?
나랑 결혼해 줄래?
Will you turn off the TV, please?
TV 좀 꺼 줄래?

items.think: When we ask "Would you please...?" we're **making a polite request**. But be careful: with a sharp tone, it can sound **annoyed**, like "Would you please be quiet?"
ex: Would you please wait here?
여기서 기다려 주시겠어요?
Would you please be quiet?
조용히 좀 해 주시겠어요?
Would you please sign here?
여기 서명해 주시겠어요?

items.think: When we ask "Would you mind...?" we're **asking very politely if something is okay**. Tricky part: if you're happy to help, answer "**No, not at all**," which means "I don't mind."
ex: Would you mind closing the door?
문 좀 닫아 주실 수 있을까요?
Would you mind waiting a moment?
잠시만 기다려 주실 수 있을까요?
Would you mind? — No, not at all.
괜찮으시겠어요? — 네, 전혀 상관없어요.

items.expr: Do you mind if I + 동사?
items.think: When we ask "Do you mind if I...?" we're **asking for permission politely**. "Do you mind if I sit here?" Again, "**No, go ahead**" means yes, it's okay.
ex: Do you mind if I sit here?
여기 앉아도 될까요?
Do you mind if I open the window?
창문 열어도 괜찮아요?
Mind if I join you?
같이 해도 될까?

items.expr: Is it okay if I + 동사?
items.think: When we ask "Is it okay if I...?" we're **asking for permission in a simple, friendly way**. It's easier than "Do you mind" because **"Yes" means yes**. Very common in daily life.
ex: Is it okay if I leave early today?
오늘 일찍 가도 괜찮을까요?
Is it okay if I bring a friend?
친구 데려가도 돼?
Is it okay if I call you tonight?
오늘 밤에 전화해도 괜찮아?

items.think: When we say "Could I get...?" we're **ordering or asking for something politely**. Native speakers use this all the time at cafés and restaurants. It sounds **much more natural than "Give me."**
ex: Could I get a coffee, please?
커피 한 잔 주시겠어요?
Could I get the check?
계산서 주시겠어요?
Could I get a bag for this?
이거 봉투 하나 받을 수 있을까요?

items.expr: I'd appreciate it if you could + 동사
items.think: When we say "I'd appreciate it if you could," we're **making a polite request and thanking them in advance**. It's great for emails and work. It sounds **respectful and professional**.
ex: I'd appreciate it if you could reply soon.
빨리 답장 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
I'd appreciate it if you kept this secret.
이건 비밀로 해 주시면 고맙겠어요.
I'd really appreciate your help.
도와주시면 정말 감사하겠어요.

items.expr: I was just wondering if + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "I was just wondering if," we're **asking something very gently**. The past tense and "just" make it **extra soft and low-pressure**. It's perfect when you don't want to bother someone.
ex: I was just wondering if you're free tonight.
혹시 오늘 밤 시간 되나 해서요.
I was just wondering if you could help me.
혹시 좀 도와주실 수 있을까 해서요.
I was wondering if I could borrow your car.
혹시 차 좀 빌릴 수 있을까 해서.

items.think: When we say "Let me...," we're **offering to do something**. "Let me help you" means I'll help. "**Let me check**" or "Let me think" means **give me a moment**.
ex: Let me help you with that.
그거 내가 도와줄게.
Let me check my schedule.
일정 좀 확인해 볼게.
Let me think about it.
생각 좀 해 볼게.

items.expr: Let me know if + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "Let me know if," we mean **tell me if this happens**. It's a friendly way to **leave the door open**: "Let me know if you need anything."
ex: Let me know if you need anything.
필요한 거 있으면 말해.
Let me know if you can come.
올 수 있으면 알려 줘.
Let me know when you arrive.
도착하면 알려 줘.

items.think: When we say "Feel free to," we're **giving permission and making someone feel comfortable**. It means you don't need to ask. "**Feel free to call me anytime**" is warm and welcoming.
ex: Feel free to ask questions.
편하게 질문하세요.
Feel free to call me anytime.
언제든 편하게 전화해.
Feel free to help yourself.
마음껏 드세요.

items.expr: Do you know where + 주어 + 동사?
items.think: When we ask "Do you know where...?" we're **asking for information more politely than a direct question**. Note the order: "Do you know where **the restroom is**?" not "where is the restroom."
ex: Do you know where the restroom is?
화장실이 어디 있는지 아세요?
Do you know where he went?
그가 어디 갔는지 알아?
Do you know what time it is?
지금 몇 시인지 알아요?

pattern.title: 💡 제안·조언·의무
pattern.core: 제안: Let's(같이 하자) → Why don't we(왜 안 해?) → How about(어때?) 순으로 부드러워진다. 의무: have to(밖에서 정해짐) > should(내 판단·조언)

items.think: When we say "Let's," we're **suggesting that we do something together**. It's **direct, positive, and energetic**. "Let's go!" "Let's take a break." "Let's not" means let's not do it.
ex: Let's go!
가자!
Let's take a break.
좀 쉬자.
Let's not talk about it.
그 얘기는 하지 말자.

items.think: When we ask "Why don't we...?" we're **making a soft suggestion**, not asking for a reason. It means "how about we do this?" "**Why don't you**..." gives advice to someone else.
ex: Why don't we eat out tonight?
오늘 저녁은 외식하는 게 어때?
Why don't we take a taxi?
택시 타는 게 어때?
Why don't you take a day off?
하루 쉬는 게 어때?

items.think: When we ask "How about...?" we're **putting an idea on the table to see what others think**. "How about pizza?" It's **light and flexible**. After "How about," use a noun or -ing.
ex: How about pizza?
피자 어때?
How about going for a walk?
산책하는 거 어때?
How about tomorrow at 7?
내일 7시 어때?

items.expr: What about + 명사 / -ing? / Then, what about ~?
items.think: When we ask "What about...?" we're often **bringing up something that was forgotten** or **offering another option**. "What about your sister?" "Then, what about Sunday?"
ex: What about your sister? Is she coming?
네 여동생은? 그녀도 와?
Then, what about Sunday?
그럼 일요일은 어때?
What about the money?
돈은 어떻게 하고?

items.think: When we ask "Why not try...?" we're **encouraging someone to try something new**. It means there's no reason not to. It's **friendly advice**.
ex: Why not try cooking at home?
집에서 요리해 보는 건 어때?
Why not try asking him directly?
그에게 직접 물어보는 건 어때?
Why not try something new?
새로운 걸 시도해 보는 건 어때?

items.think: When we ask "Have you tried...?" we're **gently suggesting a solution**. It's a soft way to give advice. "**Have you tried turning it off and on?**" is a classic.
ex: Have you tried turning it off and on?
껐다 켜 봤어?
Have you tried the new café?
새로 생긴 카페 가 봤어?
Have you tried drinking more water?
물을 더 마셔 봤어?

items.expr: You should + 동사 / I think you should + 동사
items.think: When we say "You should," we're **giving advice based on what we think is best**. Adding "I think" makes it **softer and less pushy**: "I think you should apologize."
ex: You should see a doctor.
병원 가 보는 게 좋겠어.
I think you should apologize.
네가 사과하는 게 좋을 것 같아.
You should try this cake.
이 케이크 꼭 먹어 봐.

items.think: When we say "I should probably," we mean **it's time for me to do this**. "Probably" makes it gentle. "**I should probably go**" is a polite way to say you're leaving.
ex: I should probably go now.
이제 슬슬 가 봐야겠다.
I should probably call my mom.
엄마한테 전화해야겠다.
We should probably get some sleep.
우리 좀 자야겠다.

items.pic: have to = [밖에서 정해진 의무]  /  should = [내 판단]
items.think: When we say "I have to," it's **a must, often because of rules or situations**. When we say "I should," it's **a good idea, based on my own judgment**. "Have to" is stronger.
ex: I have to work tomorrow.
나 내일 일해야 해.
You have to wear a seatbelt.
안전벨트는 꼭 매야 해.
I should exercise more.
운동을 더 해야겠어.

items.expr: I've got to / I gotta + 동사
items.pic: [해야 할 일을 가지고 있다] = have to (구어)
items.think: When we say "I've got to" or "I gotta," we mean **I have to**, but more casually. Native speakers say "**I gotta go**" all the time. It's spoken English, not formal writing.
ex: I've got to go. Talk to you later.
나 가야 돼. 나중에 얘기해.
I gotta finish this tonight.
이거 오늘 밤에 끝내야 돼.
You've got to see this!
이거 꼭 봐야 해!

items.expr: Make sure to + 동사 / Make sure (that) + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "Make sure to," we're telling someone to **check and do it for certain**. It's a friendly reminder. "**Make sure you lock the door**" means don't forget.
ex: Make sure to lock the door.
문 꼭 잠가.
Make sure you bring your passport.
여권 꼭 챙겨.
Let me make sure I understand.
제가 제대로 이해했는지 확인할게요.

items.think: When we say "Don't forget to," we're **reminding someone to do something in the future**. "To" points forward to an action that still needs to happen. "**Don't forget to call me!**"
ex: Don't forget to call me.
나한테 전화하는 거 잊지 마.
Don't forget to take your medicine.
약 먹는 거 잊지 마.
Don't forget your umbrella.
우산 잊지 마.

items.think: When we say "It's time to," we mean **now is the moment to do this**. "It's time to go to bed." It can also mean **you've waited long enough**: "It's time to say goodbye."
ex: It's time to go to bed.
잘 시간이야.
It's time to say goodbye.
작별할 시간이야.
It's time for lunch.
점심시간이야.

pattern.title: 💬 감정·반응 (감정 먼저, 이유는 나중)
pattern.core: 영어는 감정을 먼저 꺼내고(I'm sorry / Thank you / I'm happy) 그 이유를 that·for·about으로 뒤에 붙인다. 한국어 '~해서 미안해'와 순서가 반대!

items.expr: I'm sorry that + 주어 + 동사 / I'm sorry about + 명사
items.think: When we say "I'm sorry," we **put the feeling first and the reason after**. "I'm sorry that I was late." "I'm sorry about last night." We also use it to **show sympathy**: "I'm sorry to hear that."
ex: I'm sorry that I was late.
늦어서 미안해.
I'm sorry about last night.
어젯밤 일은 미안해.
I'm sorry to hear that.
그 얘기 들으니 안타깝다.

items.think: When we say "Thank you for," we **say thanks first, then the reason**. "Thank you for coming." After "for," use **a noun or -ing**. It's one of the most useful phrases in English.
ex: Thank you for coming.
와 줘서 고마워.
Thank you for your help.
도와줘서 고마워요.
Thanks for waiting.
기다려 줘서 고마워.

items.expr: I'm upset / happy that + 주어 + 동사
items.think: When we say "I'm happy that" or "I'm upset that," we **share our feeling first, then explain why**. "Upset" can mean **sad, worried, or angry**, depending on the situation.
ex: I'm happy that you're here.
네가 와서 기뻐.
I'm upset that he lied to me.
그가 나한테 거짓말해서 속상해.
She's glad that it's over.
그녀는 그게 끝나서 다행이라 여겨.

items.think: When we say "I'd be glad to," we mean **I'm happy to do it for you**. It's a warm way to **accept a request**. "Glad to meet you" is a friendly greeting.
ex: I'd be glad to help.
기꺼이 도와드릴게요.
I'm glad to hear that.
그 얘기 들으니 기쁘다.
Glad to meet you.
만나서 반가워요.

items.think: When we say "I feel bad about," we mean **I feel guilty or sorry about something I did**. It's softer than a full apology but shows **you care how the other person feels**.
ex: I feel bad about what I said.
내가 한 말이 마음에 걸려.
I feel bad about leaving early.
일찍 가서 미안한 마음이야.
Don't feel bad. It wasn't your fault.
미안해하지 마. 네 잘못 아니야.

items.think: When we say "I'm afraid," we're often **not scared at all**. It's a **polite way to give bad news**: "I'm afraid we're closed." It softens the message. ("I'm afraid of spiders" is the real fear.)
ex: I'm afraid I can't come.
아쉽지만 못 갈 것 같아.
I'm afraid we're closed.
죄송하지만 영업 끝났어요.
I'm afraid of spiders.
나 거미 무서워해.

items.expr: I hate to say this, but ~
items.pic: [이 말 하기 싫지만] + but [진짜 하고 싶은 말]
items.think: When we say "I hate to say this, but," we're **warning that something unpleasant is coming**. It shows we **don't enjoy saying it**, which makes the message feel kinder.
ex: I hate to say this, but you're wrong.
이런 말 하기 싫지만 네가 틀렸어.
I hate to say this, but we're out of time.
말하기 미안하지만 시간이 없어.
I hate to say it, but I told you so.
이런 말 하긴 싫지만, 내가 그랬잖아.

items.think: When we say "To be honest," we're **about to share our true opinion**, even if it's not what people want to hear. It's like **taking off a mask**. In casual speech: "Honestly..."
ex: To be honest, I didn't like the movie.
솔직히 그 영화 별로였어.
To be honest, I'm a little nervous.
솔직히 좀 긴장돼.
Honestly, I don't care.
솔직히 난 상관없어.

items.think: When we say "That makes sense," we mean **I understand, and it seems logical**. It's a great way to **show you're following someone's explanation**. "Does that make sense?" checks understanding.
items.ko: 말 되네, 이해가 돼, 일리 있어
ex: Oh, that makes sense now.
아, 이제 이해가 되네.
Does that make sense?
이해되셨어요?
It doesn't make sense.
그건 말이 안 돼.

items.think: When we say "That explains it," we mean **now I know why that happened**. You heard the reason, and the puzzle is solved. It's **very similar to "No wonder."**
ex: He didn't sleep last night? That explains it.
어젯밤 못 잤대? 아 그래서 그랬구나.
The power was out? That explains it.
정전이었어? 그래서 그랬구나.
That explains why she's upset.
그래서 그녀가 속상해했구나.

items.expr: I'm (not) okay with + 명사 / -ing / I'm okay
items.think: When we say "I'm okay with that," we mean **I accept it, it doesn't bother me**. "I'm not okay with it" means **I don't accept it**. "I'm okay, thanks" is a soft way to say **no thanks**.
ex: I'm okay with that.
난 그거 괜찮아.
I'm not okay with you lying to me.
네가 나한테 거짓말하는 건 용납 못 해.
More coffee? — I'm okay, thanks.
커피 더 줄까? — 난 괜찮아, 고마워.

items.expr: I'm not in the mood to + 동사 / for + 명사
items.think: When we say "I'm not in the mood," we mean **I don't feel like doing that right now**. It's about **how we feel at the moment**, not forever. "I'm not in the mood for pizza."
ex: I'm not in the mood to talk.
얘기할 기분 아니야.
I'm not in the mood for pizza.
피자 먹을 기분 아니야.
Are you in the mood for a movie?
영화 볼 기분이야?

items.think: When we say "I'm curious about," we mean **I want to know more about it**. It's a **soft, friendly way to show interest** without asking a direct question.
ex: I'm curious about your job.
네 일이 궁금해.
I'm curious about how it ended.
어떻게 끝났는지 궁금해.
Just curious, how old are you?
그냥 궁금해서 그런데, 몇 살이야?

items.think: When we say "I can't stop," we mean **I keep doing something even if I try not to**. "I can't stop laughing." "I can't stop thinking about you." It shows **a strong feeling**.
items.ko: 자꾸 ~하게 돼, ~하는 걸 멈출 수가 없어
ex: I can't stop laughing.
웃음이 멈추질 않아.
I can't stop thinking about you.
네 생각이 계속 나.
I can't stop eating these chips.
이 과자 손이 멈추질 않아.

pattern.title: ⏳ 시간 감각 (경험·진행·변화)
pattern.core: 현재완료 have p.p. = 과거에서 지금까지 이어진 '선'. 과거의 일을 지금 손에 '가지고(have)' 있는 그림 — 한국어엔 없는 감각이다

items.think: When we ask "Have you ever...?" we're **asking about any experience in your whole life until now**. The time doesn't matter, only **whether it happened**. "Have you ever been to Japan?"
ex: Have you ever been to Japan?
일본 가 본 적 있어?
Have you ever tried sushi?
초밥 먹어 본 적 있어?
Have you seen this movie?
이 영화 봤어?

items.expr: have been to + 장소 / have been + 장소
items.think: When we say "I've been to London," we mean **I visited and came back**. It's about **experience**. "Where have you been?" asks **where you were until now**.
ex: Have you been to Jeju?
제주도 가 본 적 있어?
I've been to London twice.
런던에 두 번 가 봤어.
Where have you been?
어디 갔다 왔어?

items.think: When we say "I've been -ing," we're **talking about something that started in the past and is still happening**. "I've been waiting for an hour" means **I'm still waiting**. It shows a continuing action.
ex: I've been waiting for an hour.
한 시간째 기다리고 있어.
I've been studying English lately.
요즘 계속 영어 공부하고 있어.
It's been raining all day.
하루 종일 비가 오고 있어.

items.think: When we say "has been + past participle," we mean **something was done to it, and it's still that way now**. "The meeting has been canceled." The focus is **on the result**, not who did it.
ex: The meeting has been canceled.
회의가 취소됐어.
I've been invited to the party.
나 그 파티에 초대받았어.
This house has been sold.
이 집은 팔렸어.

items.think: When we say "I've been busy -ing," we're **explaining what kept us busy**. "I've been busy working" is a common reason **why you haven't called or replied**.
ex: I've been busy working.
일하느라 바빴어.
I've been busy getting ready for the trip.
여행 준비하느라 바빴어.
She's busy with her kids.
그녀는 애들 돌보느라 바빠.

items.expr: It's been + 기간 + since + 주어 + 과거동사
items.think: When we say "It's been ... since," we're **measuring time from a past moment until now**. "It's been two years since I moved here." "**It's been ages!**" means long time no see.
ex: It's been a long time since we met.
우리 만난 지 정말 오래됐다.
It's been two years since I moved here.
여기 이사 온 지 2년 됐어.
It's been ages!
진짜 오랜만이다!

items.think: When we say "I just finished," we mean **I completed it a moment ago**. "Just" means **very recently**. "I just finished eating" means you're done right now.
ex: I just finished my homework.
방금 숙제 끝냈어.
I just finished eating.
방금 다 먹었어.
We just finished the project.
우리 방금 프로젝트 끝냈어.

items.think: When we say "I just realized," we mean **something suddenly became clear to me**. It's like a light bulb turning on. "**I just realized I left my phone at home!**"
ex: I just realized I left my phone at home.
방금 폰 집에 두고 온 거 알았어.
I just realized it's Friday!
오늘 금요일인 거 방금 깨달았어!
I just realized how late it is.
이렇게 늦은 줄 이제 알았네.

items.expr: I forgot to + 동사 / I almost forgot
items.think: When we say "I forgot to," we mean **I didn't do something I was supposed to do**. "I almost forgot" means **I nearly forgot, but I remembered just in time**.
ex: I forgot to call you back.
너한테 다시 전화하는 걸 깜빡했어.
I almost forgot your birthday!
네 생일 깜빡할 뻔했어!
Oh, I almost forgot. Here's your book.
아, 깜빡할 뻔했다. 여기 네 책.

items.think: When we say "I keep -ing," we mean **this happens again and again**, often in an annoying way. "I keep forgetting his name." "**Keep going!**" means don't stop.
ex: I keep forgetting his name.
그 사람 이름을 자꾸 까먹어.
My phone keeps turning off.
폰이 자꾸 꺼져.
Keep going! You're almost there.
계속 가! 거의 다 왔어.

items.think: When we say "I'm getting...," we mean **I'm slowly changing into that state**. "I'm getting hungry." "It's getting dark." It shows **a change in progress**.
ex: I'm getting hungry.
슬슬 배고파진다.
It's getting dark.
점점 어두워지고 있어.
I'm getting better at English.
영어 실력이 점점 늘고 있어.

items.think: When we say "I didn't mean to," we mean **it was an accident, not my intention**. It's an important phrase for apologies: "**I didn't mean to hurt you.**"
ex: I didn't mean to hurt you.
너한테 상처 주려던 건 아니었어.
Sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt.
미안, 끼어들려던 건 아니었어.
I didn't mean it.
진심 아니었어.

items.expr: Are you done with + 명사 / -ing? / I'm done with ~
